body:
The Meaning of Sulh-i-kul

Akbar governed an empire whose population included people belonging to different religions, communities and regional traditions. His authority depended partly on bringing these different groups into a political system that could maintain peace and secure cooperation.

Sulh-i-kul

Sulh-i-kul means universal peace or peace with all. It was Akbar's principle of governance that emphasised tolerance, justice and the peaceful coexistence of different religious communities under imperial authority.

The principle did not require people to abandon their existing religious beliefs. Instead, it aimed to prevent religious differences from becoming a permanent basis for political discrimination or conflict.

Abul Fazl, Akbar's close adviser and court historian, helped articulate this ideal. In the Mughal conception of enlightened kingship, the emperor was expected to protect different communities and maintain justice among them.

The ideal of religious coexistence operated within the authority of the imperial state. Freedom of religious expression was not understood as a licence to rebel against the emperor or engage in conflict with other communities.

Religious Discussions at Fatehpur Sikri

During the 1570s, Akbar held discussions with scholars and representatives of different religious traditions at Fatehpur Sikri.

These discussions took place in the Ibadat Khana, or House of Worship. Participants included Muslim religious scholars, Brahmanas, Jesuit Christian priests (from 1580) and Zoroastrians.

Akbar's exposure to different beliefs encouraged him to question the idea that the state should be guided exclusively by the interpretation of one religious group. He increasingly emphasised ethical principles such as honesty, justice and peace that could be applied across communities.

Ibadat Khana was the place associated with Akbar's interreligious discussions. Sulh-i-kul was the broader principle of governance associated with tolerance and peace. The two terms are related but do not mean the same thing.

Changes in Religious Taxation

Akbar's approach was expressed in administrative decisions as well as court discussions.

  • 1563: Akbar abolished the pilgrimage tax.
  • 1564: Akbar abolished jizya, a tax levied on non-Muslim subjects under earlier arrangements.

These changes reduced religious distinctions in taxation and supported the wider policy of political accommodation. They did not abolish land revenue or every other form of taxation.

The policy should also be placed in its historical context. Mughal practice was not identical under every emperor. Aurangzeb reimposed jizya in 1679, demonstrating that later rulers could depart from particular policies of Akbar.

Religious Accommodation and the Imperial Nobility

Sulh-i-kul complemented Akbar's policy of recruiting people from different backgrounds into imperial service. Rajputs, Iranis, Turanis, Afghans and other groups could receive positions in the administration and military hierarchy.

This connection was politically important. If the emperor relied on the service of regional elites belonging to different communities, policies that encouraged cooperation could help support imperial stability.

However, the principle of universal peace should not be interpreted as proof that every conflict disappeared. The empire continued to use military force against rulers who resisted its political authority.

Provincial Administration under Akbar

Akbar's statecraft also required an administrative structure capable of governing conquered territories. The empire was divided into provinces called subas.

  • Suba: A province of the Mughal Empire.
  • Subadar: The provincial governor responsible for the principal political and military functions of provincial government.
  • Diwan: The officer responsible for financial and revenue administration in the province.
  • Faujdar: An officer associated with military command and the maintenance of order in a territorial jurisdiction.
  • Kotwal: An officer responsible for policing and order in a town.

Distinguishing the subadar from the diwan is particularly important. The subadar exercised general political and military authority, while the diwan supervised financial matters. This division helped the emperor oversee both provincial government and revenue administration.

Abul Fazl and the Ain-i-Akbari

Akbar commissioned his court historian Abul Fazl to prepare the Akbar Nama, a history of his reign and empire.

The work comprises 3 major volumes. The first 2 are principally historical accounts, while the third is the Ain-i-Akbari.

The Ain-i-Akbari describes Akbar's administration, army, revenue arrangements, provinces and aspects of the empire's society and economy. It preserves information about the institutions through which Mughal authority was exercised.

The important distinction is that Akbar Nama is the larger work, while Ain-i-Akbari is its third volume, with particular importance for understanding Mughal administration.

How Akbar's Policies Worked Together

Akbar's success came from combining several institutions and policies rather than relying on a single measure.

  • Military expansion brought additional regions under Mughal authority.
  • Rajput alliances and accommodation incorporated regional ruling groups into the imperial structure.
  • Mansabdari defined officers' ranks and military obligations.
  • Jagirdari assigned revenue rights to support the remuneration of many officers.
  • Zabt sought systematic land revenue assessment in areas where accurate surveying was feasible.
  • Sulh-i-kul provided a principle of governance intended to encourage peaceful coexistence among different communities.
  • Provincial administration used subadars and diwans to organise political authority and financial supervision.

These arrangements were connected. Conquest enlarged the empire, revenue helped maintain its officers and armies, and political accommodation helped the emperor obtain cooperation from the people and ruling groups of different regions.

Prelims focus

  • Sulh-i-kul: Universal peace, associated with Akbar and explained by Abul Fazl.
  • Ibadat Khana: Religious discussions at Fatehpur Sikri during the 1570s.
  • 1563 and 1564: Abolition of pilgrimage tax and jizya respectively.
  • 1679: Reimposition of jizya under Aurangzeb.
  • Subadar and diwan: Provincial political-military authority and financial administration respectively.
  • Trap: Ain-i-Akbari is the third volume of Akbar Nama, not a separate work written by Todar Mal.

title: Sulh-i-kul and Akbar's Statecraft: Religion, Administration and Imperial Unity
